L297: # Emperor penguin
L298: ## On this page
L299: 
L300:   * cite240†Physical description and related species L301:   * cite241†Special adaptations to the cold L302:   * cite242†Distribution and abundance L303:   * cite243†Breeding L304:   * cite244†Diet and feeding L305:   * cite245†Huddling L306: ## Physical description and related species
L307: 
L308: Scientific name: Aptenodytes forsteri.
L309: 
L310: Emperor penguins are amazing birds. They not only survive the Antarctic winter, but they breed during the worst weather conditions on earth.
L311: 
L312: Our research aims to learn more about the penguins: how they live, where they go, what they do, and what they need to survive. We want to understand how human activities may impact on their lives and survival chances.
L313: The emperor is the largest of the 18 penguin species. Adults can weigh up to 40 kg at the start of the breeding season. Historically, there were some penguin species even larger than emperors, weighing perhaps 100 kg! These mega-penguins became extinct several tens of thousands of years ago.
L314: 
L315: Like all penguins, emperors are flightless birds.
L316: 
L317: Some emperors live to more than 40 years but most do not live that long in the wild. Their closest relatives are cite246†king penguins .
L318: Emperor penguins Photo: Barry Becker
L319: ## Special adaptations to the cold
L320: 
L321: Emperors have excellent insulation in the form of several layers of scale-like feathers – it takes very strong winds (over 60 knots or about 110 kilometres per hour) to get them ruffled. In proportion to their overall size, they have small bills and flippers to conserve heat. Their nasal chambers also recover much of the heat that is normally lost during exhalation.
L322: Emperor penguins have large reserves of energy-giving body fat and a relatively low level of activity during winter. They are very social creatures, and one of their survival mechanisms is to huddle together to keep warm. This huddling instinct means that they do not defend any territory. The emperor penguin is the only species of penguin that is not territorial.
L323: Emperor penguins have the ability to ‘recycle’ their own body heat. The arteries and veins lie close together so that blood is pre-cooled on the way to a penguin’s feet, wings and bill and warmed on the way back to the heart.
L324: 
L325: Emperors’ feet are adapted to the icy conditions. Like other animals that live in the polar regions, special fats in their feet prevent them from freezing. Emperors have strong claws for gripping the ice.
L326: Perfectly adapted feet of emperor penguin for protecting chicks on ice and webbing for swimming in open sea Photo: Eddie Gault
L327: ## Distribution and abundance
L328: 
L329: Emperor penguins breed in colonies scattered around the Antarctic continent. Colonies range in size from a few hundred to over 20,000 pairs. Most colonies are situated on the cite247†fast-ice that is locked between islands or grounded icebergs.
L330: 
L331: Conservation status: cite248†endangered†iucn.org .
L332: Emperor penguin populations are projected to undergo a moderately rapid decline over the next 3 generations owing to the effects of projected climate change. Researchers are studying the cite249†influence of climatic changes on populations and how future environmental change may impact the species.
L333: ## Breeding
L334: 
L335: Emperor penguins are the only animals that breed during the Antarctic winter.
L336: 
L337: Emperor penguin breeding cycle
L338: 
L339: The emperor has not only evolved special physical characteristics to help it survive the extreme Antarctic conditions, it has also developed some unique social behaviours such as huddling. Like most penguins, emperor parents closely share parental duties once the chicks have hatched. But only the males take on the incubation duties.
L340: Emperor penguin chicks being socialized by male parents at Auster rookery Photo: Gary Miller
L341: ## Diet and feeding
L342: 
L343: Emperor penguins are exquisite divers! While they mostly forage at depths of 150 to 250 metres, the deepest dive recorded was to 565 metres. On average, dives last 3 to 6 minutes but the longest dive on record was 22 minutes.
L344: Emperor penguins are near the top of the Southern Ocean’s food chain. They have a varied menu that changes with the season. Some prey items are more important than others. One of the most frequently eaten prey species is the Antarctic silverfish Pleuragramma antarcticum. They also eat other cite8†fish , Antarctic cite10†krill and some species of cite15†squid . Most prey items are small. Since they are very cold when ingested, their small size makes it easier to bring food up to body temperature to digest it.
L345: An adult penguin eats 2–3 kg per day. When they need to fatten up before a moult or at the start of the breeding season, they can eat as much as 6 kg per day.
L346: 
L347: Breeding adults have to fill up their stomachs before they return to the colony. They need to feed their chicks and the colonies are often a long way from the fishing grounds. A chick needs about 42 kg of food from each parent.
L348: 
L349: Emperor penguins entering the water from ice floe Photo: Andrew Burgess
L350: ## Huddling
L351: 
L352: Emperor penguins have to face freezing conditions including katabatic winds that blow off the polar plateau and intensify the cold. Emperor colonies also face blizzards of up to 200 km/h.
L353: 
L354: To keep warm, the males close ranks to share their warmth. When carrying their incubation fat, emperors are about as large around the chest as an average man. On very cold days, as many as 10 of them pack into every square metre of a huddle.
L355: In the huddle, individuals seem to temporarily lose their identity, and the group takes on the appearance and behaviour of a single living entity. Huddling cuts the heat loss by as much as 50%, and enables males to survive the long incubation fast. The warmer they are, the longer their fat lasts. The temperature inside a huddle can be as high as +24°C.
L356: On a social level, huddling behaviour is an extraordinary act of co-operation in the face of common hardship. Emperors take this to an extreme – taking turns to occupy the warmest and coldest positions in the huddle.
L357: On windy days, those on the windward edge feel the cold more than those in the centre and down-wind. One-by-one they peel off the mob and shuffle, egg on feet, down the flanks of the huddle to join it again on the leeward side. They follow one another in a continuous procession, passing through the warm centre of the huddle and eventually returning back to the windward edge.
L358: Due to this constant circulation, the huddle gradually moves downwind. During a 48-hour blizzard, the huddle may shift as much as 200 metres.
L359: 
L360: Emperor penguins huddle together against the cold Photo: Robyn Mundy

L298: # Weddell seal
L299: 
L300: Weddell seal near Mawson station Photo: Glenn Browning
L301: 
L302: Scientific name: Leptonychotes weddellii
L303: ## Physical description and related species
L304: 
L305: Weddell seals are large animals. Both adult males and females are about 3 metres long and weigh around 400–500 kg. The head is small relative to body size and the colour is usually dappled grey and black on the back with a mostly white under-belly.
L306: ## Distribution and abundance
L307: 
L308: Weddell seals have a circumpolar distribution and are coastal, staying around the fast ice and venturing only 15–20 km into the Southern Ocean to feed. Weddell seals haul-out onto the fast-ice to rest and moult, and for females to pup.
L309: Weddell seals are incredibly placid sedentary animals. They can be approached without much apparent stress to the animal. When they haul-out they remain close to their access hole on top of the ice. Underwater they remain relatively close to their breeding colonies, usually within 50–100 km though occasional migrations of several hundred kilometres do occur, especially by juveniles.
L310: Weddell seals are the most southerly ranging mammal to permanently inhabit the continent. Sightings of the seals have been made in New Zealand and Australia, though they are very rare indeed.
L311: ## Threats
L312: 
L313: The under-ice environment is relatively safe from air breathing predators such as cite241†killer whales and cite242†leopard seals .
L314: ## Special adaptations
L315: 
L316: Because Weddell seals breath air and live under the fast-ice, they must breath through cracks and holes in the ice cover. There are many cracks in the ice during the warmer summer months.
L317: During winter these openings freeze over and Weddell seals use their canine and incisor teeth to rasp open the new ice and so maintain holes through which to breathe. Maintaining these breathing holes results in teeth wearing down to such an extent that the animal may eventually be unable to feed or keep the precious holes open. A seal must find its way to the breathing holes before it runs out of oxygen.
L318: Their powers of navigation must be highly accurate as they must find these holes even during the darkness of winter.
L319: Conservation status: cite243†least concern†www.iucnredlist.org L320: ## Breeding
L321: 
L322: Weddell seals haul-out onto the stable fast-ice to rest and moult, and for females to pup, returning to the same area each year. Females of 6 years and over give birth in October to 1 pup per year. Pups weigh 25–30 kg at birth and mothers care for them for 6 weeks by which time they have grown to 110–140 kg. Pups learn to swim and haul-out of the water from 1 week old.
L323: During the breeding season males defend underwater territories from other males for access to breathing holes and females. Both male and female seals vocalise, males may do so to maintain established territories. The only observation of mating (Cline et al, 1971) reported that it took place under water for 5 minutes or more. The male maintained rhythmic body undulations at a rate of 160 per minute.
L324: ## Diet and feeding
L325: 
L326: Weddell seals are carnivores. Their food varies with time and location but mid-water (pelagic) and bottom dwelling (benthic) fish, squid, octopus and prawns are common. One seal was repeatedly observed to capture a fish weighing more than 40 kg. Weddell seals are very capable divers, remaining under water for up to 45 minutes and reaching depths as great as 720 m in search of prey. Lengthy shallow dives are probably exploration dives for new ice holes and food sources.
L327: ## Science
L328: 
L329: The Australian Antarctic Division has undertaken a long-term study of the Weddell seal in the Vestfold Hills near cite244†Davis station, Antarctica. The study focuses on:
L330:   * the ecological position of this seal in the Antarctic through prey studies
L331:   * population characteristics such as the composition of age classes, dispersion of the animals from their breeding sites and the degree of immigration and emigration of the Vestfolds breeding colony
L332:   * determining the influence of climate and weather on the life of Weddell seals, eg long-term fluctuation such as El Nino events and short term local climate effects on haul-out behaviour
L333:   * underwater vocalisations for geographic variation and purpose

L297: # Adélie penguin
L298: 
L299: Secret life of penguins
L300: 
L304: ## Video transcript
L305: 
L306: Adelie penguins near Casey research station have been studied for the last 60 years.
L307: Seabird Conservation Ecologist, Dr Colin Southwell: "It's a long time series, there aren't many time series in Antarctica that long. Over that time the regional population has increased by a factor of 6. So it used to be about 30,000 breeding pairs, and now it's almost 200,000 breeding pairs. That's nearly half a million breeding birds. So it's a very large population in the Windmill Islands – the third largest in East Antarctica."
L308: The penguin population grew rapidly from the 1960s to the 1990s – the question is, has that continued?
L309: Colin Southwell: "We also realised that some populations were still going gangbusters, in terms of growing at very fast rates; and some were flatlining, so they were not changing at all. What we've found is that the populations that are stable don't have much breeding habitat left. So they've expanded in their growth in previous years, and virtually filled that habitat, so they can't grow any more. We've found that the populations that have been increasing quickly have a lot of habitat left."
L310: Many of the Windmill Islands near Casey station are 'penguin heaven'.
L311: 
L312: There's space to lay eggs, surrounded by krill to eat with not too much sea ice.
L313: 
L314: Colin Southwell: "Good breeding habitat on land is ice-free land, snow-free land, not too steep, not flat – because flat gets too wet – and with lots of pebbles so they can build their nests."
L315: 
L316: 40,000 breeding Adelies live on Shirley Island alone, in less than one square kilometre.
L317: Colin Southwell: "So we can count them from helicopters flying overhead; taking photos, and counting the penguins from the photos; or, if we can get to an island, we can do a direct count from the ground. It's not a trivial task. There are tens and hundreds of thousands of penguins in this population, so it's a very difficult and time-consuming thing to do."
L318: 
L319: As well as field work, automatic cameras can spy on the penguins all year round.
L320: That's exactly what Madi did, studying 45,000 photos from Adelie colonies.
L321: 
L322: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies Honours student, Madison McLatchie: "I looked at 10 photos per day for every season, and I did 10 seasons at the 5 camera sites."
L323: 
L324: Adelie penguins use rocks to build their nests.
L325: Madi McLatchie: "Stealing rocks from other penguins, that's a major thing that they do. They'll just go take rocks, no permission asked, and then take that back to their nest. Otherwise, they'll just go scrounging for rocks around the colony as well."
L326: 
L327: From the photos, she recorded the breeding success of 450 Adelie penguin nests.
L328: 
L329: The more rocks in the nest, the better the chance of one or more chicks surviving.
L330: Madi McLatchie: "So the higher the nest's off the ground, the more likely they are to be away from the snow cover and the moisture on the ground."
L331: 
L332: It seems obvious, but the results were a surprise.
L333: 
L334: Madi McLatchie: "We weren't expecting that nest structure would have such a big impact on breeding success, because that was a relatively new finding. Only a few people prior to me have found that."
L335: 
L336: Knowing about nests is all part of a bigger picture beyond the cameras.
L337: Colin Southwell: "We've been focusing on Adelie penguins all this time, but the penguins are part of a larger ecosystem. What we're trying to understand is how that larger ecosystem works."
L338: 
L339: They're indebted to the people who keep the cameras going and collect the images.
L340: Madi McLatchie: "All the expeditioners who went down in that 10 year period I was looking at – I need to thank them so much for giving me and other people the opportunity to find out as much as we can about Adelie penguins to help them into the future."
L341: 
L342: [end transcript]

L344:

L353: 
L354: Scientific name: Pygoscelis adeliae
L355: 
L356: Adélie penguins were discovered in 1840 by scientists on the French Antarctic expedition led by explorer Jules Dumont d’Urville. D’Urville named Adélie Land, in southern Antarctica, after his wife, Adéle. Scientists Jacques Hombron and Charles Jacquinot also attributed this name to the species.
L357: ## Physical description
L358: 
L359: Adélie penguins are medium sized penguins, weighing 3 to 6 kg and standing 70 cm tall. They are distinguished by the white ring surrounding the eye. Males and females are of similar size and difficult to tell apart.
L360: Like all penguins, Adélies are excellent swimmers. They are also very determined and successful long distance walkers travelling across many kilometres of fast ice on the return journey to their colonies. Their walking speed on ice averages 2.5 km/h and swimming speed 4 to 8 km/h. When enough snow covers the ice, they prefer to plonk onto their bellies and toboggan.
L361: 
L362: They are closely related to the cite247†gentoo (Pygoscelis papua) and the cite248†chinstrap (Pygoscelis antarctica) penguins.
L363: ## Distribution and abundance
L364: 
L365: Adélie penguins are one of only 5 species of penguins that live on the Antarctic continent (Adélie, cite249†emperor , cite250†gentoo , cite251†chinstrap and cite252†macaroni penguins).
L366: 
L367: Adélie penguins breed around the entire Antarctic coast and small islands in places where there is exposed rock. Many of these locations are close to the Australian cite253†research stations .
L368: cite254†Long-term population research focuses on the Windmill Islands near Casey, home to the third largest Adélie population in East Antarctica. Scientists have shown the colonies here have increased from 30,000 breeding pairs in the 1950s to nearly 200,000 today. A small colony of about 1,800 breeding pairs are studied on Béchervaise Island near Mawson, as part of a long term cite255†ecosystem monitoring program .
L369: Scientists know much more about the behaviour of Adélies in the warmer months, because they breed on land between October and February. Less is known about their behaviour in the winter where they spend time at sea in the pack ice. Scientists are tracking their routes so they can find out exactly where the Adélies go on their long sea journeys. So far, scientists know that these penguins can swim more than 1,200 km away from their breeding site.
L370: Their main predators are cite256†leopard seals , and also cite257†skuas who take eggs and chicks from breeding colonies.

L375: ## Breeding
L376: 
L377: In spring, Adélie penguins build nests out of the pebbles they find on dry land. They choose a sloping site so that, when the snow melts, water runs away from the nest. When the pack ice has not yet broken up, finding food nearby can be a problem. Adélies may have to walk over 50 km across the ice to reach the sea. Individuals always return to the same nest and the same mate, if they can.
L378: By mid-November there are 2 eggs in the nest. Parents take turns to incubate the eggs and find food. The first 2 incubation shifts tend to last 11 to 14 days and are followed by shorter shifts. The chicks hatch in December and the parents alternate guard and feeding duties swapping every few days. The adults catch fish, cite10†krill and other small crustaceans, which they regurgitate for their chicks. The chicks on Béchervaise Island put on around 80 grams per day.
L379: In January, when chicks are 3 weeks old, they are big enough to be left alone. This allows both parents to simultaneously collect food for them. When the parents are away the chicks group together for protection and warmth.
L380: In February, the chicks replace their down with adult feathers. At the age of 7 to 9 weeks they are ready to go to sea. Most chicks will not return to the breeding colony until they are 3 to 5 years of age and capable of breeding. Adélie penguins have a life expectancy of 10 to 20 years.

L385: ## Diet and feeding
L386: 
L387: The diet of Adélies differs according to the location where food is captured. Local meals (those within 20 km of the colony) consist mostly of fish, amphipods and ‘crystal krill’ (Euphausia crystallorophias), while offshore meals consist of mainly ‘cite10†Antarctic krill ’ (Euphausia superba). Meal sizes range from about 300 to 650 g depending on the size of the chicks.
L388: Breeding adults swim between 5 to 120 km offshore to catch food for their chicks. Feeding trips range from 5 to 72 hours in duration.
L389: 
L390: Some Adélie penguins are capable of diving to depths of up to 175 m but usually feed within the upper 70 m of the water column.

L393: ## Adélie satellite tracking
L394: 
L395: Scientists have attached cite259†satellite transmitters to selected Adélies so they can track their movements when out at sea feeding. The transmitters send signals to an orbiting satellite which relays the signals to the Australian Antarctic Division at Kingston, Tasmania. The sea routes of the penguins can then be mapped. Scientists often use dive depth recorders as well to determine how deep the penguins dive to catch their prey.
L396: ## Automated Penguin Monitoring System
L397: Australian scientists have revolutionised the gathering of data from penguins. Before the new method was in place, scientists had to handle penguins repeatedly to obtain the data required. Now, the cite260†Automated Penguin Monitoring System is used to automatically weigh, identify and determine the direction of penguins as they walk across a weighing platform placed between the breeding colony and the sea. This method of gathering data ensures the least disturbance and is less stressful for the penguins.
L398: To identify each bird, scientists use a tiny electronic tag which they implant under the skin of the penguins. As the birds step onto the platform, their tag activates the system. Readings can then be obtained of how long each bird has been away foraging and how much food the bird gives to its chick. The weighing of penguins is important, as scientists can then tell how much krill and fish they are eating and delivering to their chicks.
